analysis.one_liner: Requires nursing homes to report COVID-19 cases and deaths daily, sends protective gear, testing, and strike teams to facilities, and renews elder-abuse programs.
analysis.headline: Introduced by the Senate Finance chairman with three Republican cosponsors in July 2020, the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote before that Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required nursing homes and long-term care facilities to publicly report COVID-19 cases and deaths daily, including who died by age, race, and ethnicity. It would have redirected a portion of federal COVID-19 relief money to buy protective equipment, provide free testing for residents and staff, and fund rapid-response 'strike teams' for facilities with outbreaks. It would also have reauthorized funding through 2023 for state long-term care ombudsman programs, adult protective services, and elder-abuse forensic centers, and made it easier to flag facilities with repeated abuse or neglect problems.
analysis.who_benefits: Nursing home and long-term care residents, whose deaths made up a large share of America's early COVID-19 toll, would gain from transparent case and death reporting, free testing, protective equipment, and faster help during outbreaks. Facility workers would gain from the same protections and free testing. Victims of elder abuse and neglect would gain from renewed ombudsman, adult protective services, and forensic-center funding, and families would get clearer ratings about which facilities are safe.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nursing home residents, their families, and care workers

how_it_helps.text: Facilities must report suspected and confirmed COVID-19 cases and all deaths daily to the Secretary, and the data must be posted publicly with demographic detail such as age, race, and ethnicity [S2].

A portion of COVID-19 relief funds must be used for protective equipment and regular free testing for residents and staff of skilled nursing facilities, Medicaid nursing facilities, and assisted living facilities [S2].

Relief funds must also support statewide 'strike teams' that respond to outbreaks, and must alert state enforcers and the Medicaid fraud control unit if a facility has safety problems that immediately endanger residents [S3].

The bill reauthorizes through FY2023 grants for long-term care ombudsman programs ($12 million a year), elder-abuse forensic centers ($10 million a year), and state adult protective services, plus $60 million in direct payments to state and tribal protective services during the emergency [S2].
Residents are guaranteed access to telephones and video communication with family, including staff help using the technology, during the emergency [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Nursing home and long-term care operators bear new daily reporting duties, public posting of their case and death counts, published lists of chronically problematic facilities, and a review that could weight abuse records and fines more heavily in the public star ratings. Some COVID-19 relief money is redirected from other purposes, so other recipients of relief funding bear an opportunity cost.
analysis.who_pays_short: Nursing home operators and other relief-fund recipients

drawbacks.text: The bill reroutes money from future COVID-19 relief appropriations 'notwithstanding the original purpose,' overriding whatever Congress had already directed those funds toward [S3].

Many provisions are studies, reports, and reviews — a comprehensive review of the Five-Star rating system, an evaluation of abuse-reporting protocols, and a disparities task force — rather than immediately enforceable care standards [S3].
Strike teams could include state militia members and other designees, an emergency staffing mechanism that relies on state oversight and confidentiality rules rather than clinical licensure [S3].
Operators would face real administrative costs from daily case, death, and staffing data reporting, a burden smaller facilities would feel most.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to a uniquely vulnerable population — transparent death counts, protective equipment, testing, outbreak response, and elder-abuse funding — are concrete and large; the costs are mostly compliance burden on facilities and a modest redirection of relief money. The bill's main weakness is that many of its strongest-sounding provisions are studies and reviews rather than binding rules, so even if enacted, much would have depended on the administration following through.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee in July 2020, and sat there with no committee action and no floor vote before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on July 2, 2020, and was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
No further action was taken; the complete action history ends with the referral to Finance [S5].
The bill's sponsor, Chuck Grassley, chaired the Senate Finance Committee in that Congress, so the committee where the bill sat was the committee he led.
Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and bills not passed by then expire.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing home operators were better off because the bill died: they avoided daily public reporting of cases and deaths, published lists of chronically poor performers, and a review that could have penalized bad records in the star ratings. Residents, families, and elder-abuse programs gained nothing.

for.name: Chuck Grassley
for.role: U.S. Senator (R-IA); Chairman, Senate Finance Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on July 2, 2020, and referred it to the Finance Committee he chaired, which took no further action on it.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never held a markup or vote on it.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote during the COVID-19 relief negotiations of 2020.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so the partisan split was never tested; the sponsor and all three cosponsors were Republicans, and no Democratic position on the bill is in the record.

industries.industry: Nursing home and long-term care operators
industries.note: The bill sends operators relief-funded protective equipment, free testing, and strike-team help with outbreaks, which they want. But it also requires daily public reporting of cases and deaths, publishes lists of chronically troubled facilities, and could reweight the star ratings toward abuse records and fines — the transparency side of the bill is exactly what the industry has historically resisted, and avoiding it is the main gain from the bill dying.

industries.industry: State and tribal adult protective services and ombudsman programs
industries.note: The bill renews and increases their grant funding through FY2023 and sends $60 million in emergency payments directly to them, with no state matching requirement.

A portion of future COVID-19 appropriations is redirected to nursing home protective equipment, testing, and strike teams regardless of the funds' original purpose, reducing what is available for other relief uses.
